topics.title: Meaning of Agricultural Technology and Ways of Land Cultivation (Primary 4)
topics.content:
SOCIAL STUDIES
RELIGION AND NATIONAL VALUES
THIRD TERM
WEEK 11
PRIMARY 4
THEME: AGRICULTURE
PREVIOUS LESSON - Meaning (Types) and Effects of Pollution (Primary 4)
TOPIC - AGRICULTURAL TECHNOLOGY
LEARNING AREA
1. Meaning of Agricultural Technology
2. Traditional and Modern Farming
PERFORMANCE OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, the pupils should have attained the following objectives (cognitive, affective and psychomotor) and should be able to:
1. explain the meaning of agricultural technology.
2. state the different between traditional and modern farming.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
Chart showing traditional and modern tools.
Video clips of traditional and modern farmers working on their farm.
METHOD OF TEACHING - Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
Scheme of Work
9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
Course Book
All Relevant Material
Online Information
Relevant links - Third Term Scheme of Work and Plan Lesson Note for Social Studies Primary 4 Primary 5 and Primary 6 Links
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON ONE - INTRODUCTION
Agriculture involves cultivation of land, farming, and rearing of animals.
MEANING OF AGRICULTURAL TECHNOLOGY
Agricultural Technology is the used of technology (machines like tractors, planters, harvesters, etc.) for land cultivation, farming and rearing of animals.
WAYS OF LAND CULTIVATION
Traditional Ways of Land Cultivation
Traditional farming is the used of simple farm tools like hoes, cutlass, baskets, hooks, fishing nets, etc. This method is complete used of simple tools for growing crops, rearing of animals, fishing, etc.
Modern Ways of Land Cultivation
Modern farming is the used of modern tools like tractor and ploughing instead of hoes and cutlass, harvester, fertilizer, insecticide and pesticides, trawler, etc.
REVISION AND WEEK 11 LESSON ASSESSMENT
As stated in performance objectives or lesson evaluation.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions;
2. Guides pupils to identify and make a list of agricultural products and tools;
Pupil’s Activities - Identify and make a list of agricultural products and tools.
3. Leads and explains the meaning of agricultural technology;
Pupil’s Activities - Explain the meaning of agricultural products.
4. Guides and leads the pupils to differentiate between traditional method and modern modern of farming;
Pupil’s Activities - Differentiate between traditional method and modern modern of farming.
CONCLUSION
- To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
- Assignment
- Find out the uses of tractor, ploughing, fertilizer, pesticides and insecticide.
- Visit a farm near to you and find out their ways of farming.
- Next Lesson - Advantages and Disadvantages (Problems) of modern farming.
LESSON EVALUATION
Pupils to:
1. Explain the meaning of agricultural technology.
2. Differentiate between traditional and modern farming.

AGRICULTURE

FIRST TERM
WEEK 2
PRIMARY 4
THEME - AGRICULTURE
PREVIOUS LESSON - Third Term Agriculture Plan Lesson Notes for Primary 3 (Basic 3)
TOPIC: LAND AND SOIL
LEARNING AREA
1. Introductory Activities
2. Meaning of Land
3. Meaning (Types) of Soil
4. Lesson Evaluation and Weekly Assessment (Test)
PERFORMANCE OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, most of the pupils should have attained the following objectives -
1. differentiate between land and soil.
2. list soil types.
ENTRY BEHAVIOR
The pupils can identify and state the importance of land and soil.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of soil samples - sandy, clayey and loamy.
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
Scheme of Work
9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
Course Book
All Relevant Material
Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
LESSON 1 - INTRODUCTION
Soil is one of the essential components of land. It consists of particles of rock, different kinds of soil and organic material.
Land is the surface area of the earth which is not covered by water.
MEANING OF LAND
Land is the solid part of the earth not covered by water.
MEANING OF SOIL
Soil is the upper layer of the earth where plants grow.
There are three (3) major soil,
- Sandy soil
- Clay soil
- Loamy soil
LESSON 2 - TYPES OF SOIL
1. CLAY SOIL
Clay soil is the solid parts of the soil used for moulding and building of houses.
2. SANDY SOIL
Sandy soil is the loose parts of the soil used for building of houses and construction of roads.
2. LOAMY SOIL
Loamy soil is the best parts of the soil used for growing crops.
It combines the good parts of clay and sandy.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
1. To introduce the lesson, the teacher revises the previous lesson. Based on this, he/she asks the pupils some questions;
2. Collects soil samples to show their characteristics.
Pupil’s Activities - Observe and identify soil types.
3. Summary the key points on the board.Pupil’s Activities - Copy as the teacher writes.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Soil Types - Characteristics of Sandy Soil | Characteristics of Clay Soil | Characteristics of Loamy Soil Primary 4 (Basic 4) - Agriculture
LESSON EVALUATION
Ask pupils to -
1. Differentiate between land and soil?
2. Mention 3 types of soil.
WORKBOOK
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT (TEST)
1. _____ is the solid part of the earth not covered by water.
A. Soil
B. Earth
C. Land
2. _____ is the upper layer of the earth where plants grow.
A. Soil
B. Earth
C. Land
3. There are _____ types of soil.
A. Two
B. Three
C. Four
4. _____ is the loose parts of the soil used for building of houses and construction of roads.
A. Loamy soil
B. Sandy soil
C. Clay soil
5. _____ is the best parts of the soil used for growing crops.
A. Loamy soil
B. Sandy soil
C. Clay soil
6. _____ Clay soil is the solid parts of the soil used for moulding and building of houses.
A. Loamy soil
B. Sandy soil
C. Clay soil
7. The mixture of clay and sandy is _____.
A. Loamy soil
B. Sandy soil
C. Clay soil
8. _____ is one of the essential components of land.
9. Land is the _____ of the earth which is not covered by water.
A. surface area
B. top area
C. lower area
10. Land is the surface area of the earth which is not covered by _____.
A. soil
B. rock
C. water

topics.title: Preservation of Farm Produce: Meaning of Preservation and Reasons for Preserving Farm Produce Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 2 Agriculture
topics.content:
PRESERVATION OF FARM PRODUCE: MEANING OF PRESERVATION AND REASONS FOR PRESERVING FARM PRODUCE
AGRICULTURE
PRIMARY 6 - FIRST TERM - WEEK 2
THEME - PREVOCATIONAL STUDIES
PREVIOUS LESSON - First Term, Second Term and Third Term Agriculture Plan Lesson Notes and Scheme of Work for Primary 5 (Basic 5)
TOPIC - PRESERVATION OF FARM PRODUCE
LEARNING AREA
1. Introduction
2. Meaning of Preservation of Farm Produce
3. Reasons for Preserving Farm Produce
4. Importance of Preserving Farm Produce
5. Weekly Assessment: Test Questions and Answers/Assignment
6. Summary
LEARNING OBJECTIVES
By the end of the lesson, pupils should be able to:
1. Explain the meaning of preservation of farm produce.
2. Mention examples of farm produce that can be preserved.
3. State the reasons for preserving farm produce.
4. Explain the importance of preserving farm produce.
5. Identify ways preservation helps farmers and consumers.
ENTRY BEHAVIOUR
Pupils have previously learned about harvesting and post-harvesting activities.
This lesson builds on that knowledge by teaching pupils how farm produce can be preserved after harvesting to prevent spoilage, reduce wastage, and keep the produce useful for a longer period.
INSTRUCTIONAL MATERIALS
The teacher will teach the lesson with the aid of:
1. Samples or pictures of farm produce such as yam, maize, cassava, tomatoes, fruits, and vegetables
2. Pictures or charts showing preserved farm produce
3. Samples of dried or processed farm produce
4. Agriculture textbook
METHOD OF TEACHING
Choose a suitable and appropriate methods for the lessons.
Note - Irrespective of choosing methods of teaching, always introduce an activities that will arouse pupil’s interest or lead them to the lessons.
REFERENCE MATERIALS
1. Scheme of Work
2. 9 - Years Basic Education Curriculum
3. Course Book
4. All Relevant Material
5. Online Information
CONTENT OF THE LESSON
INTRODUCTION
Farm produce is harvested for food, sale, and other uses. However, some farm produce can spoil quickly if it is not properly handled after harvesting.
For example, fresh tomatoes, fruits, vegetables, fish, and meat can deteriorate when they are not properly preserved. Preservation helps to keep farm produce safe and useful for a longer period.
In this lesson, pupils will learn about the meaning of preservation of farm produce, the reasons for preserving farm produce, and its importance to farmers and consumers.
MEANING OF PRESERVATION
Preservation of farm produce is the process of treating and storing harvested farm products in ways that prevent or slow down spoilage and keep them safe and useful for a longer period.
Examples of Farm produce such as yam, cassava, maize, tomatoes, vegetables, fruits, meat, and fish can spoil when they are not properly preserved.
REASONS FOR PRESERVING FARM PRODUCE
Farm produce is preserved for the following reasons:
1. To prevent spoilage: Preservation slows down the activities of microorganisms and other causes of deterioration.
2. To extend shelf life: It helps farm produce remain usable for a longer period.
3. To reduce wastage: Preservation reduces the amount of produce lost after harvesting.
4. To maintain quality: Proper preservation helps retain the quality of farm produce.
5. To ensure availability: Preserved produce can be kept for use when it is not readily available.
6. To improve food security: It helps provide food beyond the immediate harvest period.
7, To increase income: Farmers can preserve produce and sell it later when prices may be more favourable.
8. To facilitate transportation: Some preservation methods make produce easier to transport over longer distances.
9. To provide food during the off-season: Preserved produce can be used when the crop is out of season.
10. To support processing and marketing: Properly preserved produce can be stored until it is processed or taken to the market.
IMPORTANCE TO FARMERS AND CONSUMERS
Preservation is important because it:
- Helps farmers store produce for later sale.
- Can increase farmers’ income.
- Makes food available for longer periods.
- Improves food security.
- Makes transportation and marketing easier.
- Reduces losses after harvesting.
WEEKLY ASSESSMENT: TEST QUESTIONS AND ANSWERS/ASSIGNMENT
A. Multiple Choice Questions
1. What is preservation of farm produce?
A. The process of planting crops
B. The process of selling farm produce
C. The process of preventing or slowing down spoilage
D. The process of harvesting crops
2. Which of the following is an example of farm produce that can be preserved?
A. Stone
B. Sand
C. Maize
D. Plastic
3. One major reason for preserving farm produce is to ______.
A. Increase spoilage
B. Destroy food
C. Reduce food availability
D. Reduce wastage
4. Preservation helps farm produce to remain useful for a ______.
A. Longer period
B. Single day
C. Few minutes
D. Shorter period
5. How can preservation benefit farmers?
A. It prevents them from harvesting crops.
B. It can help them store produce for later sale.
C. It destroys their produce.
D. It reduces the quality of their produce.
B. Fill in the Gaps
6. Preservation helps to prevent farm produce from ______ quickly.
7. Preservation reduces the ______ of farm produce after harvesting.
8. Preserved farm produce can be kept for a ______ period.
9. Preservation helps provide food during the ______ season.
10. Farmers can preserve produce and sell it later to increase their ______.
C. True or False
11. Preservation helps to reduce spoilage of farm produce. ______
12. Preservation increases the wastage of farm produce. ______
13. Preserved farm produce can be stored for future use. ______
14. Preservation can help maintain the quality of farm produce. ______
15. Farm produce should never be preserved. ______
D. Matching
16. Food security - A. Amount of farm produce lost after harvesting
17. Preservation - B. Keeping produce useful for a longer period
18. Spoilage - C. Food becoming unfit or less suitable for use
19. Wastage - D. Period when a particular crop is not normally available
20. Off-season - E. Availability of sufficient food for people
ANSWER KEY
1. C 2. C 3. D 4. A 5. B
6. Spoiling
7. Wastage
8. Longer
9. Off
10. Income
11. True
12. False
13. True
14. True
15. False
16. Food security - E. Availability of sufficient food for people
17. Preservation - B. Keeping produce useful for a longer period
18. Spoilage - C. Food becoming unfit or less suitable for use
19. Wastage - A. Amount of farm produce lost after harvesting
20. Off-season - D. Period when a particular crop is not normally available
SUMMARY
Pupils learned that preservation of farm produce is the process of preventing or slowing down spoilage so that farm produce can remain useful for a longer period.
They learned that farm produce is preserved to reduce wastage, extend shelf life, maintain quality, ensure food availability, provide food during the off-season, increase farmers’ income, and improve food security.
PRESENTATION
To deliver the lesson, the teacher adopts the following steps:
Step 1: Introduction
The teacher asks pupils:
- What happens to farm produce when it is not properly handled after harvesting?
- Can fresh tomatoes and fruits remain fresh forever?
- What can a farmer do to keep farm produce for a longer period?
The teacher explains that some farm produce can spoil quickly after harvesting. Preservation helps to prevent or slow down spoilage and keeps the produce useful for a longer period.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer the questions and mention examples of farm produce that can spoil.
Step 2: Meaning of Preservation of Farm Produce
The teacher explains that preservation of farm produce is the process of preventing or slowing down the spoilage of harvested farm products so that they can remain safe and useful for a longer period.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain the meaning of preservation of farm produce in their own words.
Step 3: Examples of Farm Produce That Can Be Preserved
The teacher explains that different farm products can be preserved.
- Examples include: Maize, Yam, Cassava, Beans, Tomatoes, Fruits, Vegetables, Fish, Meat
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils mention farm produce that can be preserved.
Step 4: Reasons for Preserving Farm Produce
The teacher explains that farm produce is preserved to:
- Prevent or reduce spoilage.
- Reduce wastage.
- Extend the shelf life of produce.
- Maintain the quality of produce.
- Make produce available for future use.
- Provide food during the off-season.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils state reasons for preserving farm produce.
Step 5: Importance to Farmers and Consumers
The teacher explains that preservation is important because it:
- Helps farmers store produce for later sale.
- Can increase farmers’ income.
- Makes food available for longer periods.
- Improves food security.
- Makes transportation and marketing easier.
- Reduces losses after harvesting.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils explain how preservation benefits farmers and consumers.
Step 6: Examples of Preserved Farm Produce
The teacher gives examples of preserved products:
- Dried maize
- Dried vegetables
- Dried fish
- Smoked fish
- Dried cassava
- Stored yam
- Processed fruits
The teacher explains that different preservation methods are suitable for different types of farm produce.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils identify preserved farm products they have seen or used.
Step 7: Group Activity
The teacher divides pupils into four groups:
- Group 1: Define preservation of farm produce and mention five examples.
- Group 2: State five reasons for preserving farm produce.
- Group 3: Explain five importance of preservation to farmers.
- Group 4: Explain five importance of preservation to consumers.
The teacher guides the groups and allows each group to present its answers.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils discuss, write, and present their answers to the class.
Step 8: Lesson Summary
The teacher reviews the meaning, reasons, and importance of preserving farm produce.
Pupils’ Activities: Pupils answer oral questions and summarise the lesson.
Step 9: Evaluation
The teacher gives pupils a different set of 20 questions as oral questions, a quiz, take-home work, or a quick test to assess their understanding of the preservation of farm produce.
Pupils’ A ctivities: Pupils answer the questions individually or in groups.
CONCLUSION
To conclude the lesson for the week, the teacher revises the entire lesson and links it to the following week’s lesson.
NEXT LESSON
Methods of Persevering Farm Produce Primary 6 (Basic 6) First Term Week 3 Agriculture
LESSON EVALUATION
Teacher asks pupils,
1. What is preservation of farm produce?
2. Mention five farm products that can be preserved.
3. State four reasons for preserving farm produce.
4. Mention four importance of preserving farm produce.
5. How does preservation help farmers and consumers?
